content: The turnaround time for pyrazinamide susceptibility testing using molecular methods is faster compared to phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). However, the acceptability of such tests depends on their ability to accurately detect mutations associated with pyrazinamide resistance. In certain settings, clinicians and laboratory staff may require further clarification and justification for prioritizing this specific drug test, especially since it is not currently part of routine DST. This prioritization may be necessary to avoid delays and to obtain critical drug resistance information. The feasibility of implementing the pyrazinamide line probe assay (LPA) is challenged by the significant training and laboratory infrastructure required. Additionally, the availability of an automated interpretation system is crucial, as the results are complex and difficult to interpret manually. High-complexity hybridization-based nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for detecting pyrazinamide resistance present specific challenges, including the difficulty of interpreting results due to the large number of bands generated. Local epidemiological data on resistance prevalence should guide testing algorithms, and pretest probability is important for clinical interpretation of results. The cost of such tests varies depending on factors such as the number of samples in a batch, staff time, and other parameters, necessitating a local cost analysis. Tests with low, moderate, and high complexity require progressively greater technical competency, staff qualifications, and time, which impacts planning and budgeting. The availability and timeliness of local support services and maintenance should also be considered when selecting a provider. Laboratory accreditation and compliance with a robust quality management system, including appropriate quality control, are essential for sustained service excellence and trust. Training of both laboratory and clinical staff is critical to ensure effective service delivery and clinical impact. The use of connectivity solutions for communicating results is encouraged to improve service efficiency and reduce the time to treatment initiation. In all settings, pyrazinamide resistance is significantly associated with rifampicin resistance. Implementing high-complexity hybridization-based NAATs requires laboratories with adequate infrastructure, space, and functional sample referral systems. Due to the manual steps involved, well-trained staff are needed to set up assays and maintain instruments. Special training and experience are required to interpret banding patterns on the test strips. Further research is needed to evaluate the impact of specific mutations on treatment outcomes among patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). Studies should also focus on the integration and optimization of diagnostic technologies within the broader landscape of testing and care, as well as diagnostic pathways and algorithms. Economic studies evaluating the costs, cost-effectiveness, and cost-benefit of diagnostic technologies are necessary. Qualitative studies should assess equity, acceptability, feasibility, and end-user values of diagnostic technologies. Additionally, the interpretation of results from high-complexity hybridization-based NAATs should be compared with sequencing and newer evidence on genotypic and phenotypic associations. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis emphasize the importance of rapid diagnostics for tuberculosis detection. Systematic reviews are commissioned to evaluate the performance and use of diagnostic tools or methods. The certainty of evidence is assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, which provides a framework for translating evidence into recommendations. The certainty of evidence is rated as high, moderate, low, or very low, reflecting varying levels of confidence in the estimates. If systematic review evidence is unavailable or limited, potential effects can be modeled for diagnostic accuracy, cost, and cost-effectiveness. For example, disease prevalence combined with test sensitivity and specificity can estimate the number of false positives and negatives in a population. Similarly, economic and epidemiological data can be used to estimate and model expenditures and cost-effectiveness ratios. Qualitative evidence on end-user perspectives may be generated through interviews if public data are scarce. This evidence-to-recommendation process informs domains such as feasibility, accessibility, equity, and end-user values.
